title: The third vow: make much of food
theme: The third rule — make food abundant, or hold it in high esteem — with earth and space as food and eater, each resting in the other.

words.context: Śaṅkara: make it abundant; Kūranārāyaṇa and Gopālānanda: hold it in high esteem
a rule of life for the one who knows Brahman this way (Śaṅkara on 3.7)
Śaṅkara (on 3.7): stands firm as food and eater
Śaṅkara (on 3.6): having food in abundance — not merely having some, which anyone has
Śaṅkara (on 3.6): one who eats food, whose fire burns bright

words.meaning: by the lustre of sacred learning
words.context: Śaṅkara (on 3.6): the radiance that comes from self-control and knowledge

morphology.note: Optative middle of kṛ, ‘one should make’; with bahu, ‘make abundant’ (Śaṅkara) or ‘make much of’, esteem highly (Kūranārāyaṇa, Gopālānanda, Madhva: bahu manyeta).
Masculine here, agreeing with ākāśaḥ (in 3.7 and 3.8 neuter, with śarīram and jyotiḥ).

translation.literal: One should make food abundant. That [is] the vow. The earth indeed [is] food; space [is] the eater of food. In the earth space is established; in space the earth is established. So this food is established in food. He who knows this food established in food is established. He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food. He becomes great — by offspring, by cattle, by the lustre of sacred learning; great by fame.
translation.readable: Make much of food: that is the vow. The earth is food, and space eats it; space rests in the earth, and the earth rests in space. So food rests in food. Whoever knows that food rests in food stands firm, has food and enjoys it, and grows great in family, wealth, learning and good name.

syntax: The frame of 3.7–3.8 again: an optative injunction (annaṃ bahu kurvīta), named a vow; the identifications (pṛthivī vā annam, ākāśo ’nnādaḥ); the two sentences of mutual support; the summary; the result and the refrain.

ambiguities.topic: ‘Make much food’ or ‘make much of food’?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the vow is to produce food in abundance, for one who meditates on water and light as food and eater — «अप्सु ज्योतिः इत्यब्ज्योतिषोरन्नान्नादगुणत्वेनोपासकस्य अन्नस्य बहुकरणं व्रतम्». Kūranārāyaṇa: making much of it means honouring it — «बहुकरणं सम्माननम्» — receiving it gladly («अहो मया दिष्ट्या तल्लब्धम्»). Rāmānanda: treating even a little as enough — «पर्याप्तमिति बुद्ध्या सत्कुर्यात्»; Gopālānanda (modern): «अन्नं बहु कुर्वीत बहु मन्वीत इति». Madhva’s verse has «बहु मन्येत».

ambiguities.topic: How do earth and space rest in each other?
ambiguities.note: Rāmānanda: space is the cause of earth through wind and the rest, and a cause is present in its effect — «आकाशश्च कारणं पृथिव्याः वाय्वाद्यनुक्रमेण» — while the effect rests subtly in its cause. Kūranārāyaṇa reads it of the worlds: the oblation offered on earth reaches the beings of the sky, and rain from the sky sustains the earth.

Kūranārāyaṇa sees an order in the three vows: the person (breath and body), the lights (water and fire), and now the worlds — «एवमध्यात्मम् अधिज्योतिषं चान्नं प्रतिष्ठितम् इत्युक्तम्», «अथाधिलोकं वक्तुमाह».

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose: a vow, an identification of food and eater, their mutual support, and the refrain of results shared with 3.6–3.10.

beginner: The third rule could mean two things, and the commentators divide. Taken literally it says: make food plentiful — grow it, store it, have enough to share. Most of the commentators take it more inwardly: make much of food, value it, be glad of even a little. Either way the attitude is the opposite of blame and refusal. The text then widens its view to the whole world: the earth is food, and space, which holds it, is the eater; space rests in the earth, and the earth rests in space. So, once more, food rests in food. The three rules together move outward, the commentators note, from the body to the elements to the worlds, showing everything held up by something else.
analogy: Like a host who sets a small dish on the table as if it were a feast, and so makes it one.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Make food abundant; that is the vow. The earth is food and space is the eater; space rests in the earth and the earth rests in space; so food rests in food. Whoever knows this is established, has food, eats it, and becomes great in offspring, cattle, learning and fame.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads it as abundance: the one who meditates on water and light as food and eater takes the vow of making food plentiful — «अप्सु ज्योतिः इत्यब्ज्योतिषोरन्नान्नादगुणत्वेनोपासकस्य अन्नस्य बहुकरणं व्रतम्».

commentary.q: How do the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators read ‘much’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Kūranārāyaṇa: ‘making much’ is honouring — «बहुकरणं सम्माननम्» — receiving it with words like ‘how fortunate I am to have it’, «अहो मया दिष्ट्या तल्लब्धम्». Earth and space, on which all life depends, are themselves to be honoured: «किञ्च पृथिव्याकाशयोः नित्योपजीव्यत्वात् तयोः बहुमानः कर्तव्यः». Rāmānanda: regarding even a little as enough. Gopālānanda (modern): ‘make much’ means ‘think much of’.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s verses name the Lord ‘earth’ for his vastness and ‘space’ for his knowing all — «स विष्णुः पृथिवीनामा पृथुत्वात्», «आकाशः सर्ववेत्तृतः» — and give the two vows of 3.7 and 3.9 together: «अन्नाख्यं तं नैव निन्द्याद् बहु मन्येत तं सदा». One should think of Janārdana as ‘much’ in every way: «बह्वित्येव जनार्दनम्».

advaita.text: A vow of making food abundant — «अन्नस्य बहुकरणं व्रतम्» — for the one who meditates on water and light as food and eater; like the others, it belongs to the praise of food as the door to Brahman.

visistadvaita.text: To make much of food is to honour it, and with it the earth and sky on which life depends; Kūranārāyaṇa ends that the worshipper of the supreme Self must hold food in high regard — «सर्वस्य परमात्मोपासकस्य अन्नं बहुमानं कर्तव्यम्».

dvaita.text: Earth and space are names of Viṣṇu; the vow is to hold him, named ‘food’, in high esteem — «अन्नाख्यं तं नैव निन्द्याद् बहु मन्येत तं सदा».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara alone reads bahu kurvīta literally, ‘make abundant’; the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators and Madhva read ‘esteem highly’. They differ again on what is esteemed: food as a means, the world as the Lord’s body, or the Lord himself.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s mutual nourishing of gods and men, cited by Kūranārāyaṇa on this anuvāka for earth and sky sustaining each other.
The Chāndogya’s praise of food as greater than strength, a close relative of the Taittirīya’s vows honouring food.

contemporary.text: Two readings, two lessons: produce enough to share, and value what you have. Both resist the habit of treating food as cheap and disposable. The second reading, ‘think even a little enough’, is a quiet answer to the sense that there is never enough. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What would change if you treated what you have as enough?
reflect.deeper: Śaṅkara reads ‘make much food’; the others read ‘make much of food’. Which is harder, and which comes first?
reflect.practice: Share a meal, or part of one, with someone this week, and notice how it changes the meal.

references.text: The results (annavān annādo bhavati …) repeat those of 3.6; the commentators say so (‘as before’).
Madhva’s digital text gives one comment for 3.8–3.9 (see 3.8).

flags.note: bahu kurvīta: ‘make abundant’ (Śaṅkara) or ‘esteem highly’ (Kūranārāyaṇa, Rāmānanda, Gopālānanda, Madhva).
